items.ask: List the board steps for analysing a quadratic f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx.
items.answer: 1) Gradient ∇f = Hx + b. 2) Solve Hx* = −b. 3) Hessian H. 4) Eigenvalues classify x*. 5) Eigenvectors give the contour axes through x*. 6) Sketch the contours, longest axis along the eigenvector with the smallest |λ|.
items.cue: Gradient, Solve, Hessian, Eigen, Sketch. Contours stretch farthest where the curvature is gentlest.

items.ask: Define positive definite, positive semidefinite and indefinite for a symmetric matrix H.
items.answer: Positive definite: xᵀHx > 0 for all x ≠ 0 (all λᵢ > 0). Positive semidefinite: xᵀHx ≥ 0 for all x (all λᵢ ≥ 0). Indefinite: xᵀHx takes both signs (eigenvalues of both signs).
items.cue: Read the eigenvalue signs: all up, all up or flat, mixed.

items.ask: What contour shapes go with a positive definite Hessian, an indefinite Hessian, and a singular positive semidefinite Hessian with b in the range of H?
items.answer: Positive definite: nested ellipses centred on the minimizer. Indefinite: hyperbolas whose asymptotes cross at the saddle. Singular semidefinite: parallel straight lines, a valley with a line of minimizers along the null eigenvector.
items.cue: Bowl gives ellipses, saddle gives hyperbolas, trough gives straight parallel lines.

items.ask: For a singular H ⪰ 0 with null eigenvector v, how does the linear term b decide the outcome?
items.answer: Check bᵀv. If bᵀv = 0 (b in the range of H), Hx = −b has a whole line of minimizers. If bᵀv ≠ 0, f is linear along v and unbounded below.
items.cue: A flat valley floor: a level floor holds a line of minima, a tilted floor slides to −∞.

items.ask: For H = [[a, c],[c, a]], state the eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
items.answer: λ₁ = a + c with v₁ = (1, 1)/√2; λ₂ = a − c with v₂ = (1, −1)/√2. The contour axes lie at ±45 degrees through the critical point.
items.cue: Equal diagonals: the sum direction gets a + c, the difference direction gets a − c.

items.ask: State Sylvester's criterion for a symmetric H to be positive definite.
items.answer: H ≻ 0 exactly when every leading principal minor is positive: H₁₁ > 0, det of the top-left 2×2 block > 0, and so on up to det H > 0.
items.cue: Climb the diagonal staircase: every top-left square determinant stays positive.

items.ask: Find and classify the stationary points of f = x² − y² + y⁴.
items.answer: ∇f = (2x, −2y + 4y³). (0, 0): H = diag(2, −2), a saddle. (0, ±1/√2): H = diag(2, 4), two strict minimizers with f = −¼.
items.cue: Double well: the quartic wins far out, the negative quadratic wins near zero, a saddle hump sits between two minima.

items.ask: State the strong Wolfe conditions with their typical constants.
items.answer: 1) Armijo: f(x + αp) ≤ f(x) + c₁α∇fᵀp. 2) Strong curvature: |∇f(x + αp)ᵀp| ≤ c₂|∇fᵀp|. 0 < c₁ < c₂ < 1, c₁ = 10⁻⁴, c₂ = 0.9 for Newton and quasi-Newton, 0.1 for nonlinear CG.
items.cue: Armijo caps the long step, curvature floors the short step: a window around the floor of φ(α).

items.ask: Distinguish exact and inexact line search.
items.answer: Exact: α minimizes φ(α) = f(x + αp) along p (closed form on a quadratic). Inexact: α satisfies acceptance tests such as Armijo or Wolfe, which give global convergence at low cost.
items.cue: Exact lands on the valley floor; inexact lands anywhere inside the Wolfe window.

items.ask: Give the backtracking line search algorithm.
items.answer: Start with α = 1. While f(x + αp) > f(x) + c₁α∇fᵀp, set α ← ρα with ρ ∈ (0, 1), for example ρ = ½. Return α once Armijo holds.
items.cue: Try the full step, then halve until Armijo is satisfied.

items.ask: Define a descent direction and give the steepest descent direction and update.
items.answer: p is a descent direction when ∇fᵀp < 0. Steepest descent uses p = −∇f, so x_{k+1} = x_k − α_k∇f_k; −∇f/‖∇f‖ minimizes ∇fᵀp over unit vectors.
items.cue: Downhill means a negative slope: the dot product with the gradient is below zero.

items.ask: With exact line search, what is the angle between successive steepest descent directions, and why?
items.answer: 90 degrees. At the exact minimizer along p_k, φ'(α) = ∇f_{k+1}ᵀp_k = 0, so the new gradient is orthogonal to the previous direction. This produces the zigzag on elongated contours.
items.cue: Walk until your path is tangent to a contour, then turn through a right angle.

items.ask: State the steepest descent convergence rate in function value with exact line search on a convex quadratic.
items.answer: f(x_{k+1}) − f* ≤ ((κ − 1)/(κ + 1))² (f(x_k) − f*), with κ = λ_max/λ_min. κ = 1 (circular contours) converges in one step.
items.cue: Squared ratio because the f error is quadratic in the x error. Circles: one step home.

items.ask: For f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx with g = Hx + b, give the exact steepest descent step length.
items.answer: α* = gᵀg/(gᵀHg), from setting dφ/dα = 0 along p = −g.
items.cue: Slope squared over curvature along the gradient. Dimension check: α scales as 1/H.

items.ask: Give the search direction for Newton, modified Newton, quasi-Newton (BFGS) and nonlinear CG.
items.answer: Newton: ∇²f p = −∇f. Modified Newton: (∇²f + E)p = −∇f, E making the matrix positive definite. Quasi-Newton: Bp = −∇f, B from BFGS. CG: p₊ = −∇f₊ + βp, Fletcher-Reeves β = ∇f₊ᵀ∇f₊/(∇fᵀ∇f).
items.cue: Exact curvature, repaired curvature, learned curvature, remembered direction.

items.ask: Give the local convergence rate of steepest descent, BFGS and Newton.
items.answer: Steepest descent: linear. BFGS: superlinear. Newton: quadratic, near x* with ∇²f(x*) ≻ 0.
items.cue: Gradient, secant, exact Hessian: digits grow steadily, then faster, then double each step.

items.ask: What condition keeps the BFGS matrix positive definite, and what in the line search guarantees it?
items.answer: The curvature condition yᵀs > 0. The Wolfe curvature condition ∇f₊ᵀp ≥ c₂∇fᵀp guarantees it.
items.cue: The slope along the step increases from start to end: positive curvature measured along s.

items.ask: How many iterations does linear CG need on an n-dimensional quadratic with H ≻ 0 in exact arithmetic?
items.answer: At most n, because the directions are H-conjugate (pᵢᵀHpⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j). With r distinct eigenvalues, at most r iterations.
items.cue: One conjugate direction per dimension, each minimized once and for all.

items.ask: Describe one quasi-Newton iteration.
items.answer: 1) Solve Bp = −∇f (or p = −B⁻¹∇f via the inverse update). 2) Wolfe line search for α. 3) Form s = αp and y = ∇f₊ − ∇f. 4) Update B by a low-rank formula satisfying B₊s = y, keeping symmetry and positive definiteness.
items.cue: Learn curvature from the last step: the matrix maps the step s onto the gradient change y.

items.ask: Where does the pure Newton step head when ∇²f is indefinite, and what are the two standard remedies?
items.answer: It heads to the stationary point of the quadratic model, which can be a saddle or a maximum, so p may point uphill. Remedies: modified Newton (add τI until positive definite) or a trust region.
items.cue: Newton seeks any flat spot. Lift the bowl with τI, or fence it in with Δ.

items.ask: List the steps of one trust region iteration.
items.answer: 1) Build m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp. 2) Solve min m(p) s.t. ‖p‖ ≤ Δ, approximately. 3) Compute ρ = actual/predicted reduction. 4) Update Δ from ρ. 5) Accept x + p when ρ > η.
items.cue: Model, Solve, Ratio, Resize, Accept. Trust the model only as far as it has earned.

items.ask: Interpret ρ near 1, ρ small, and ρ negative in a trust region method.
items.answer: ρ ≈ 1: model matches f; expand Δ when the step reached the boundary. ρ < ¼: poor agreement; shrink Δ. ρ < 0: f increased; reject the step and shrink Δ.
items.cue: ρ is a report card: a grade near 1 earns more trust, a failing grade shrinks the radius.

items.ask: Contrast the order of choices in line search and trust region methods.
items.answer: Line search fixes the direction first, then picks the step length. Trust region fixes the maximum step length Δ first, then picks direction and length together by minimizing the model.
items.cue: Line search: where, then how far. Trust region: how far, then where.

items.ask: Define the Cauchy point and state why it matters.
items.answer: The minimizer of the quadratic model along −g inside the trust region. Any step achieving at least a fixed fraction of the Cauchy decrease gives global convergence.
items.cue: Steepest descent inside the fence: the minimum bar every trust region step must clear.

items.ask: How does the dogleg step change as Δ grows from small to large (B ≻ 0)?
items.answer: Small Δ: along −g to the boundary. Medium Δ: on the second leg between p_U and p_B, at the boundary. Δ ≥ ‖p_B‖: the full Newton step p_B.
items.cue: The dog runs straight downhill first, then bends toward the Newton bone.

items.ask: Why can a trust region method use an indefinite B?
items.answer: The constraint ‖p‖ ≤ Δ keeps the subproblem bounded, so a minimizer exists for any B. The exact solution satisfies (B + λI)p = −g with B + λI ⪰ 0, following negative curvature to the boundary.
items.cue: The fence holds even on a saddle: the boundary catches the downhill slide.

items.ask: State the KKT conditions for min f(x) s.t. h(x) = 0, g(x) ≤ 0.
items.answer: 1) Stationarity: ∇f + λᵀ∇h + μᵀ∇g = 0. 2) Primal feasibility: h = 0, g ≤ 0. 3) Dual feasibility: μ ≥ 0. 4) Complementary slackness: μᵢgᵢ = 0.
items.cue: SPDC: Stationary, Primal, Dual, Complementary. Picture the gradient of f balanced by the pushes of the active walls.

items.ask: Define active and inactive inequality constraints at x*.
items.answer: Active: gᵢ(x*) = 0, the point sits on the wall. Inactive: gᵢ(x*) < 0, and complementary slackness gives μᵢ = 0. Equality constraints are always active.
items.cue: Touching the wall means active; standing clear of it means zero force.

items.ask: Interpret a large multiplier μᵢ.
items.answer: It is a shadow price: df*/dcᵢ = −μᵢ for gᵢ ≤ cᵢ. A large μᵢ means relaxing that constraint slightly improves f* a lot; that constraint is expensive.
items.cue: The multiplier is the price tag on the wall: high price, big payoff for moving it.

items.ask: State LICQ and its role.
items.answer: The gradients of all equality constraints and all active inequality constraints at x* are linearly independent. It is a constraint qualification: at a local minimizer it guarantees KKT multipliers exist and are unique.
items.cue: Every active wall pushes in its own independent direction.

items.ask: Give the geometric (convex cone) statement of KKT with inequality constraints g ≤ 0.
items.answer: −∇f(x*) = Σ μᵢ∇gᵢ(x*) with μᵢ ≥ 0 over the active set: the downhill direction lies in the cone spanned by the outward normals of the active constraints.
items.cue: Downhill points outward through the walls, trapped inside the cone of their outward normals.

items.ask: Give the procedure for solving a small KKT problem by hand.
items.answer: 1) Reason physically about which constraint each variable pushes against. 2) Guess an active set. 3) Solve stationarity plus active constraints for x and μ. 4) Check μ ≥ 0 and inactive gᵢ < 0. 5) Check second order. Revise the guess if a check fails.
items.cue: Think, guess, solve, check signs, check curvature: physics first, algebra second.

items.ask: With L = f + λᵀh + μᵀg, g ≤ 0 and minimization, what signs do λ and μ take?
items.answer: λ is free in sign. μᵢ ≥ 0, and μᵢ = 0 on every inactive constraint.
items.cue: Walls push one way, so their multipliers stay nonnegative; equality rails push either way.

items.ask: How do required lift and the governing physics enter a design optimization statement?
items.answer: As equality constraints: C_L = C_L,required (lift equals weight) and R(x, u) = 0 for the state u. Limits such as C_L ≤ C_Lmax or b ≤ b_max enter as inequalities g ≤ 0.
items.cue: Physics holds exactly: equalities. Limits are fences: inequalities.

items.ask: Contrast the quadratic penalty method and the log barrier method.
items.answer: Penalty: exterior, iterates approach from the infeasible side, μ → ∞, handles equalities and inequalities. Barrier: interior, iterates stay strictly feasible (g < 0), μ → 0⁺, handles inequalities.
items.cue: A penalty fines you after you cross the fence; a barrier is an electric fence felt from inside.

items.ask: What role does μ play in a barrier method?
items.answer: A homotopy parameter: each subproblem minimizes φ(x; μ) with μ held fixed, then μ is reduced toward 0 and the previous solution warm-starts the next. The minimizers trace the central path to x*.
items.cue: Fixed within each subproblem, shrinking between them: a staircase down to zero along the central path.

items.ask: What happens to the Hessian of the quadratic penalty function as μ → ∞, and what is the remedy?
items.answer: It becomes ill-conditioned, with eigenvalues of order μ along the constraint normals. Remedy: the augmented Lagrangian, which converges at finite μ by updating λ, or an exact penalty.
items.cue: Steep walls and a flat floor form a canyon. Adding λ shifts the floor so a moderate wall suffices.

items.ask: Outline one SQP iteration.
items.answer: 1) At x_k form a QP: quadratic model of L (∇²ₓₓL or BFGS) with linearized constraints. 2) Solve for p and new multipliers. 3) Line search on a merit function such as the ℓ1 penalty. 4) Update x, λ and the Hessian approximation.
items.cue: SQP is Newton's method applied to the KKT conditions: linearize, solve the QP, step, check merit.

items.ask: Give the multiplier estimates recovered from a quadratic penalty on h and a log barrier on g.
items.answer: Quadratic penalty f + (μ/2)Σhⱼ²: λⱼ ≈ μhⱼ(x(μ)). Log barrier f − μΣln(−gᵢ): μᵢ ≈ −μ/gᵢ(x(μ)), positive since gᵢ < 0.
items.cue: Match ∇φ to ∇L term by term and read off the multiplier.

items.ask: List the steps of building a linear-in-the-parameters surrogate from first principles.
items.answer: 1) Choose basis functions: ŷ = Σ wⱼφⱼ(x) = Φw. 2) Define the error e = y − Φw. 3) Minimize Σ eᵢ² = ‖e‖². 4) Set the gradient to zero: ΦᵀΦw = Φᵀy. 5) Check dimensions and rank. 6) Validate (cross-validation, R²).
items.cue: Basis, error, square, differentiate, check, validate: a regression ladder from model to verdict.

items.ask: Define a surrogate that is linear in the parameters.
items.answer: ŷ depends linearly on the coefficients w, while the basis functions φⱼ(x) may be nonlinear in x. Example: ŷ = w₀ + w₁x + w₂x² is linear in w.
items.cue: The weights enter as plain multipliers; x can be as curved as you like.

items.ask: Write the least squares error in summation and vector form, and its gradient.
items.answer: E = Σᵢ (yᵢ − Σⱼ wⱼφⱼ(xᵢ))² = (y − Φw)ᵀ(y − Φw). ∂E/∂w_k = −2Σᵢ (yᵢ − Σⱼ wⱼφⱼ(xᵢ)) φ_k(xᵢ); vector form ∇E = −2Φᵀ(y − Φw) = 0 gives ΦᵀΦw = Φᵀy.
items.cue: The chain rule on a square brings down a 2; the inner derivative brings Φᵀ to the front.

items.ask: Give the dimensions of Φ, w, y, ΦᵀΦ and Φᵀy for n samples and m basis functions.
items.answer: Φ: n × m. w: m × 1. y: n × 1. ΦᵀΦ: m × m. Φᵀy: m × 1.
items.cue: Rows are samples, columns are basis functions; ΦᵀΦ is square in the basis count.

items.ask: For full rank Φ, give the solution in the three cases n = m, n > m and n < m.
items.answer: n = m: square invertible Φ, interpolation w = Φ⁻¹y. n > m: overdetermined, least squares w = (ΦᵀΦ)⁻¹Φᵀy. n < m: underdetermined, infinitely many exact fits; take the minimum norm w = Φᵀ(ΦΦᵀ)⁻¹y or regularize.
items.cue: Equal: invert. More data: least squares. More unknowns: the shortest w that fits.

items.ask: State the ridge regression optimization problem and its solution.
items.answer: min_w ‖y − Φw‖² + λ‖w‖² with λ > 0. Solution: (ΦᵀΦ + λI)w = Φᵀy, invertible for every λ > 0, including when n < m.
items.cue: Penalize big weights; λI lifts every eigenvalue of ΦᵀΦ above zero.

items.ask: Describe k-fold cross-validation of a surrogate.
items.answer: Split the n samples into k groups. For each group, fit on the other k − 1 groups and predict the held-out group. Average the prediction errors (for example RMSE). k = n is leave-one-out.
items.cue: Every point takes a turn as the exam question the model has yet to see.

items.ask: How many coefficients does a full quadratic response surface in k variables have?
items.answer: (k + 1)(k + 2)/2: 1 constant, k linear, k pure quadratic and k(k − 1)/2 interaction terms. k = 2 gives 6, so at least 6 samples.
items.cue: Choose 2 from k + 2 slots: a triangular number, 6 for two variables.

items.ask: Give the three convexity characterizations of f in order.
items.answer: Zeroth order (definition): f(θx + (1 − θ)y) ≤ θf(x) + (1 − θ)f(y), θ ∈ [0, 1]. First order: f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x). Second order: ∇²f(x) ⪰ 0 everywhere.
items.cue: Chord above, tangent below, curvature upward: zero, one, two derivatives.

items.ask: When is min f s.t. h = 0, g ≤ 0 a convex problem, and what follows?
items.answer: f convex, every gᵢ convex, every hⱼ affine. Then every local minimizer is global, and under a constraint qualification such as Slater the KKT conditions are necessary and sufficient.
items.cue: Convex bowl, convex fences, straight rails: one valley, and KKT certifies it.

items.ask: Define a convex set.
items.answer: S is convex when θx + (1 − θ)y ∈ S for all x, y ∈ S and θ ∈ [0, 1]: the segment joining any two points stays inside S.
items.cue: Stretch a string between any two points; it stays in the room.

items.ask: Compare finite differences, complex step and the adjoint for a gradient in n variables.
items.answer: Forward FD: n + 1 evaluations, O(h). Central FD: 2n evaluations, O(h²). Complex step: n complex evaluations, machine precision. Adjoint: one primal plus one adjoint solve per output, cost independent of n.
items.cue: FD and complex step scale with inputs; the adjoint scales with outputs.

items.ask: How does the total finite difference error behave as h decreases?
items.answer: Truncation error falls (O(h) forward, O(h²) central) while subtractive cancellation error grows like ε_f/h, so the total error is V-shaped with its minimum near h ≈ √ε_f for forward differences.
items.cue: Two errors on a seesaw: truncation drops, roundoff climbs; the bottom of the V is the sweet spot.

items.ask: Define a Pareto optimal design.
items.answer: x* is Pareto optimal when every other feasible design that improves one objective worsens at least one other objective. The Pareto optimal set maps to the Pareto front in objective space.
items.cue: On the front, every gain costs something: trade-offs all the way along.

items.ask: Which portions of a Pareto front does the weighted sum reach, and which method traces all of it?
items.answer: The weighted sum reaches the convex portions, the points a tilted straight line can touch. The ε-constraint method traces the whole front, including nonconvex portions.
items.cue: A ruler pressed on the front touches the bulges; a sliding bound reaches every dent.

items.ask: Name four gradient-free methods and the core move of each.
items.answer: Nelder-Mead: reflect the worst simplex vertex through the centroid. GA: selection, crossover and mutation on a population. PSO: velocities pulled toward personal and swarm bests. Simulated annealing: accept uphill moves with probability exp(−Δf/T).
items.cue: Shape, genes, flock, metal: the simplex flips, populations breed, birds swarm, metal cools.

items.ask: List the steps of one genetic algorithm generation.
items.answer: 1) Evaluate fitness. 2) Select parents (tournament or roulette). 3) Crossover to form children. 4) Mutate with small probability. 5) Form the new population, with elitism keeping the best.
items.cue: Evaluate, select, cross, mutate, replace: survival of the fittest in five beats.

items.ask: Contrast the MDF and IDF architectures.
items.answer: MDF: optimizer handles x; a full MDA runs at every iterate, so every iterate is multidisciplinary feasible, with the fewest variables. IDF: coupling targets yᵗ become design variables with consistency equality constraints; disciplines run in parallel; consistency holds at convergence.
items.cue: MDF: Make Disciplines Fit every step. IDF: Individual Disciplines, made consistent at the end.

items.ask: How do you read an N² diagram?
items.answer: Disciplines sit on the diagonal. Outputs leave along the row, inputs arrive down the column. Entries above the diagonal are feed-forward, entries below are feedback, and feedback loops require an iterative MDA.
items.cue: Rows send, columns receive. Upstairs flows forward; downstairs flows back and forces a loop.

items.ask: Name and contrast three MDA solution methods.
items.answer: Gauss-Seidel: sequential, each discipline uses the newest coupling values. Jacobi: every discipline uses the previous iterate, so all run in parallel. Newton: solves the coupled residual system with the full Jacobian, quadratic convergence.
items.cue: Gauss-Seidel passes the baton, Jacobi starts everyone at once, Newton takes the whole Jacobian.

items.ask: Define resolution III, IV and V for two-level fractional factorial designs.
items.answer: III: main effects aliased with two-factor interactions. IV: main effects clear of two-factor interactions, which alias with each other. V: main effects and two-factor interactions clear of each other, aliased with third order and higher.
items.cue: Aliased orders sum to the numeral: III is 1 + 2; IV is 1 + 3, 2 + 2; V is 1 + 4, 2 + 3.

items.ask: Describe Latin hypercube sampling with n samples in k variables.
items.answer: Divide each variable range into n equal intervals and place the n samples so each interval of each variable holds exactly one sample, then improve spacing with a criterion such as maximin distance.
items.cue: Rooks on a chessboard: one per row, one per column, spread out.
